newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: South Korea's first hostile takeover bid fizzles out.
newsitem.headline: South Korea's first hostile takeover bid fizzles out.

text.p: South Korea's first ever hostile takeover bid appears to have fizzled out after a large shareholder, facing pressure from conglomerates' lobbying, turned against a raider group targetting a leading retailer.

Sungwon Group, once regarded as a partner of Shindongbang Corp in a bid to take over Midopa Department Store Co, said over the weekend it would sell all its 12.6 percent stake to the Dainong Group, Midopa's parent.
Dainong's purchase of 1.87 million shares in the nation's major retailer chain would be made at 42,000 won ($47.8) per share, far above the stock's last closing price of 23,400 won.
The deal would raise the stake of Dainong Group, a second-tier conglomerate engaged in textiles manufacturing and retailing, to a comfortable 45.5 percent.
"The takeover drama has now drawn to an end as Shindongbang appeared to have lost necessary support from a major shareholder," said a Hyundai Securities broker.
Edible oil producer Shindongbang, along with its joint venture Dongbang Peregrine Securities and Korea Industrial Co, holds a combined 15.6 percent stake in Midopa.
Korea Industrial is not an affiliate of Shindongbang but its president is a brother of the Shindongbang chairman.
The surprise Sungwon-Dainong deal followed a warning by the Federaton of Korean Industries against hostile takeovers.
The federation, a lobbying group representing the interests of the nation's industrial conglomermates, or chaebol, said last week it might intervene to prevent Shindongbang from taking over Midopa.
Midopa operates 21 stores across the country, including a flagship department store in Seoul's most fashionable shopping district near Myongdong.
"We have to actively defend against any hostile takeover bid," Sohn Byung-doo, a senior federation official told reporters.
South Korea introduced new rules in January to make hostile takeovers possible but many people still believe the concept is unethical.
The federation urged Shindongbang to compromise with Dainong, warning it would intervene to help stave off the takeover bid.
In a quick admission of its defeat, Shindongbang said over the weekend it had considered offering tenders to buy Midopa shares but decided not to do so.
"After consultations, both parties (Shindongbang and Dainong) will maintain a friendly, developmental and cooperative relationship," said a Shindongbang statement.
Analysts said the Midopa case would make hostile takovers, particularly those involving chaebol, virtually impossible in the near future.

"Chaebol will make full use of public aversion of hostile takeovers and corporate predators would have to concentrate on smaller firms in the short-term," an analyst with a local brokerage firm said, asking not to be identified.

The takeover talk sent Midopa's share price rocketing from a 1997 low of 16,300 won in early January to a high of 47,500 won in early March. It later fell on belief the takeover would eventually fail.
